e.etymology: A respelling of Sadie, an English pet form of Sarah, Hebrew for princess or noblewoman.
A Greek patronymic, daughter of Briseus. In Homer's Iliad Briseis is the captive whose seizure from Achilles sets off his quarrel with Agamemnon; the 2004 film Troy brought the name new attention.
A spelling of Arley, an English place name and surname usually read as eagle clearing. Once a man's name, as for Admiral Arleigh Burke, it now goes mostly to girls as part of the -leigh fashion.
namesakes: Arleigh Burke (US Navy admiral, namesake of a destroyer class)

e.etymology: The Croatian and Slovene form of Charles, from a Germanic word for a free man. In the US it also appears as a K spelling of Italian Carlo.
A modern American spelling that reads either as Jolie, French for pretty, or as Jo joined to Leigh.
Hebrew for doe or gazelle. It comes from the phrase ayelet hashachar, doe of the dawn, in the heading of Psalm 22, a poetic name for the morning star.

e.meaning: bright, cool or good, depending on the kanji
e.etymology: A Japanese name, properly Ryo with a long o, written with any of several single characters meaning bright, cool and refreshing, good, or distant.
A modern American blend of Sky or Skylar with the -lan ending of Dylan and Rylan.
The feminine of Munir, from Arabic munir, giving light, built on nur, light.
A respelling of Ivory, the English word for the creamy white material of elephant tusks, from Latin ebur. Ivory has been a given name in the US since the 1800s.
A name used in Mexico and by Mexican American families, in the group of Itzel and Itzayana. Its source is not settled; it is close to the Basque name Itziar.
From Sanskrit adya, first or primordial, a title of the goddess Durga as Adya Shakti, the original power. Aadhya is the more common spelling.
A Yiddish pet form of Yechezkel, the Hebrew original of Ezekiel, God strengthens. It is used mainly in Hasidic and other Orthodox Jewish communities.
From Sanskrit samaya, time, also an appointed moment or an agreement. It is the everyday Hindi word for time.
The English word for one who strides, and a surname. In The Lord of the Rings, Strider is the name Aragorn goes by as a ranger; more recently it recalls Atlanta Braves pitcher Spencer Strider.

assoc.t: Aragorn's ranger alias in The Lord of the Rings

e.etymology: A respelling of Jersey, the Channel Island that gave its name to New Jersey, to a knit fabric and sports shirts, and to a breed of dairy cow. The island's name is Norse, ending in ey, island.
A recent American name, close in sound to Ava, Avia and the Hebrew name Aviya. It has no settled source.
A respelling of Barrett that writes the nickname Bear into the name. Barrett is an English surname, probably from a Middle English word for strife or trouble.
A modern American name that extends Roman or Rome with the -ani ending of Armani and Imani. Romani is also an Italian surname meaning Roman, and the name of the Romani people.

assoc.t: the Romani people and their language

e.note: Romani is the name of an ethnic group, the Romani people, and of their language.

e.etymology: A surname and place name. The Holston River of Virginia and Tennessee is named for Stephen Holstein, an 18th-century settler, and the name fits the fashion for Colston, Kolton and Houston.
The English word for a two in cards and dice, from Old French deus, two. It is a traditional nickname for a son who is a second or junior, as with Jayson Tatum's son Deuce.
namesakes: Deuce McAllister (New Orleans Saints running back)
e.note: Deuce is also crude slang for a bowel movement, as in dropping a deuce.

assoc.t: deuce, a two in cards or dice; slang for a bowel movement

e.etymology: A recent American coinage in the pattern of Alayah, Malaya and Kalaya, with the Ca- beginning of Cali and Camila.
A recent American name in the sound family of Makai, Zakai and Kai. It has no settled source.
A short form of James, the English form of Latin Iacomus, from Hebrew Yaakov, Jacob, traditionally read as holder of the heel or supplanter. Jim has been everyday English since the 1800s.
namesakes: Jim Morrison (lead singer of The Doors)

e.etymology: A combination of Rose and Anna, also spelled Rosanna. Anna is the Latin form of Hebrew Hannah, grace.

Welsh taran means thunder, and Lloyd Alexander used Taran for the hero of his Chronicles of Prydain. The US peak in the early 1990s matches child actor Taran Noah Smith of Home Improvement. Taran is also a Punjabi Sikh name.
namesakes: Taran Killam (Saturday Night Live cast member)
Taran (hero of The Chronicles of Prydain and Disney's The Black Cauldron)

e.etymology: A Low German form of Christian, follower of Christ, used in northern Germany and Denmark and also spelled Karsten. In the US it sits alongside Carson and Carter.
In English a spelling of Derek, from Theodoric, an old Germanic name meaning ruler of the people. In Polish, Darek is the everyday short form of Dariusz, the Polish Darius.
The initials C.J. used as a name in their own right, usually standing for a first and middle name pair such as Christopher James, or for a junior.
namesakes: C.J. Cregg (press secretary on The West Wing)

e.etymology: An English and Irish surname from Piers, the medieval English form of Peter, from Greek petros, rock. Pierce is the more common spelling for a first name.
In 19th-century American records Amil is a spelling of Emil, from the Roman family name Aemilius. Today it is more often the Arabic name Amil, one who works or strives.

A minor Old Testament name, borne by a descendant of Issachar in 1 Chronicles. It ends in El, God; the first part is read variously as founded, taught or seen by God. Today it is used mostly in Hispanic families.
